To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the binding of ALS is not restricted to lymphocytes and is not specific for the lymphoid cell membrane.

the use of a single, well-defined, high-affinity monoclonal antibody (mAb), in combination with flow cytometry, can be used to detect the presence of ALS in the serum of patients with autoimmune disease.

the use of ALS in the preparation of [125I] IgG preparations for the study of cell surface immunoglobulins, may result in the binding of the antibody to the cell surface and that this binding can be reduced by the use of a non-lysing cell separation procedure, such as the use of a density gradient.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the interaction between ALS and the cell surface, and the effect of this interaction on the lymphocyte.
the study of the binding characteristics of ALS to lymphoid cells, and of the role of this binding in the regulation of lymphocyte functions.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of the term "antibody" is a convenient way to describe the complex of antibody and its antigen.
the ALS antibody binds specifically and quantitatively to a cell surface antigen which is present on all mouse lymphoid cells, but not on erythrocytes, fibroblasts or thymic nurse cells.
there is a significant association between the presence of ALS and a diagnosis of MS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding of ALS is dependent on the immunization protocol used and that this binding is not due to an anti-idiotypic antibody.
the ALS antibody is a useful reagent for the detection of mouse lymphocytes, which has a number of advantages over other lymphocyte surface antigens.
the binding of ALS is not a simple phenomenon and is influenced by many factors such as the nature of antigen, the nature of the antibody and the nature of the cell surface.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ALS can be used as a marker to identify the lymphocytes which have been exposed to a specific antigen.
the binding of ALS antibodies to lymphocytes is not a general phenomenon but depends on the type of immunization protocol and the type of lymphoid cell used.
ALS can bind to the surface of lymphocytes and this may contribute to the lymphopenia seen in some patients with ALS.
